title: Step Out of the Whine
concept: After this one you can cut a whine on purpose, answering from a seat the other person did not call on, so the talk turns into a real conversation instead of a row.
bookIdea: When the reply comes from a different ego state than the one addressed, the lines cross and communication breaks off until the vectors realign. The person who was crossed tends to shift into the ego state the other one invited.
bookSource: Games People Play, ch. 2; TA Today, ch. 7

opener.setting: Sunday, 21:15, your room in apartment 3B, Hawthorn Court. The Corner Table finished four hours ago, and Mum's name is on the phone for the third time this week.

lines.text: “Nobody rings me. I sit here with the TV on and I don't know what I did wrong. Tell me I didn't do anything wrong.”
lines.cue: small voice, the TV loud behind her

opener.ask: Can you answer Mum's plea from a seat she did not call on, so the call becomes a real talk instead of a row?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: How this one works: Mum's line is a plea, and every reply after it is a volley. A volley either runs on or gets cut. Tap the label that fits each line.

items.text: “Dad won't pick up, and nobody else rings. Am I that much trouble, love?”
items.cue: small and fast, the TV loud behind her
items.why: This is a plea. It asks you to soothe a hurt, and it has no plan and no verdict in it. That is the Kid, the voice that wants comfort, and it is aimed at the caring side of your Boss, the part that can soothe.

traps.0: The Boss would say “You never ring, and you know it's your own fault.” That is a verdict, so the call turns into a telling-off and the hurt never gets heard.
traps.1: The Pilot would say “Ring me on Sunday at eight and we'll talk about the week.” That is a plan, and it deals with the calls, but this line is about the hurt, so the plan misses it.

items.example:
A grandfather on a video call from his flat: “Nobody comes to see an old man. Never mind, I'll manage.”
He is asking for comfort, not for a visit timetable.

items.text: “Oh, Mum, you did nothing wrong. Don't worry about it.”
items.cue: warm and quick, reaching for the reassurance
items.prompt: What kind of reply is your line?
items.why: Your reply comes from the Caring Boss, the seat she called on, and it answers her plea with comfort. That is a matched volley, so it can run on, and she will be back with the same whine on Wednesday.

traps.1: A cut would answer from a seat she did not call on, like “What would you like from me this week?” This line does not do that. It answers her plea with comfort from the seat she called on.
traps.2: Double-talk would be a polite line with a second message under it, like “Oh, Mum, you did nothing wrong. Not that you'd believe me.” The words soothe and the tail carries a dig. Your line has no dig in it.

items.example:
A cricket WhatsApp group, a player who keeps calling himself the worst bowler: “You're not the worst, mate, don't worry.”
He gets the reassurance he was fishing for, and he will fish again on Sunday.

items.text: “What would you like from me this week, Mum?”
items.cue: calm and level, eyes on the screen, not on the TV
items.prompt: What kind of reply is your line?
items.why: This comes from the Pilot, a seat she did not call on. She called on the Caring Boss, and you asked a question instead, which is changing seat. The reply is a cut, so the whine has no seat to land in.

traps.0: A matched volley would be “Oh, Mum, you did nothing wrong.” She gets the comfort she asked for, and the whine comes back next Sunday.
traps.2: Double-talk would be the same words said through your teeth, “Of course, Mum, what would you like from me this week?” with a sigh behind it. The words are fine and the tone carries a second message, and she would hear the tone first.

items.example:
A neighbours' building group chat, the secretary upset about the lift repair: “Fine, you're upset. What do you want us to decide tonight?”
The question turns the sulk into a choice.

items.text: “Of course you're busy, love. Busy people don't ring. I know.”
items.cue: sweet voice, a sigh at the end
items.prompt: Look at what the line says and what sits under it. Which label fits Mum's line?
items.why: The first message is sweet: she knows you are busy. The second sits underneath and says you never ring. Two messages in one line is double-talk, and the sigh tells you which one is loud.

traps.0: A matched volley is a plain line that gets a plain reply from the seat it was aimed at, like “Yes, Mum, I'm busy, I'll ring Sunday.” Her line says one thing and carries a second underneath, so it is not plain.
traps.1: A cut is a reply that answers from a different seat. Mum is not switching seats here. She is carrying two messages in the same line.

items.example:
A school parents' group, a mother left out of the trip plan: “No, no, you all go ahead. I know my place.”
The first message is polite. The second is the bill, and everyone reads that one.

items.title: Sunday, 21:20, your room in apartment 3B
items.setting: The Corner Table is four hours behind you. The call has run four minutes. Mum has said “nobody” twice, and the TV is still on in her kitchen, 600 km away.

beats.text: “Nobody rings me. Dad doesn't even look at the phone. Tell me I didn't do anything wrong.”
beats.cue: voice thin, a spoon clinking in a cup

lines.text: “Tell me one thing you want from this week, Mum. Just one.”
lines.outcome: Mum stops mid-sigh. “Ring on Sundays. Properly, not for one minute.” The plea has a request in it now.
lines.why: You answered from your Pilot, a seat she did not call on, and asked for a real request. The cut stops the plea without starting a row.

lines.text: “Oh, Mum, you did nothing wrong. Don't worry about it.”
lines.outcome: She sighs, relieved. “Thank you, love. You always understand.” The plea will be back on Wednesday.
lines.why: You answered from the Caring Boss, the seat she called on. It is a matched volley, so it runs on and feels kind, and nothing is asked of her.

lines.text: “I'll ring every night, Mum, I promise. I'll fix everything this month.”
lines.outcome: Her voice warms. “Every night? You'll be tired, I know. You still owe me three weeks of calls.”
lines.why: You took on a rescue, and she has noticed the promise and started the count. That is a trap move, so the scene ends here.

beats.text: “After everything I gave up for you, you don't even ask how I manage.”
beats.cue: sharper now, a laugh with no fun in it

lines.text: “Which part of the week was hardest, Mum? Give me the day and the thing.”
lines.outcome: Mum pauses. “The Tuesday, with the electricity bill. Nobody told me it was due.”
lines.why: Her line came from the Boss and landed on your Kid. A question from your Pilot is a cut, so she has to answer with facts, and the guilt has nothing to push against.

lines.text: “I know, Mum. I'm a terrible son. I'm sorry.”
lines.outcome: “Yes, well, you should be,” she says, and the call goes soft for a minute.
lines.why: You answered her Boss with your Kid. The sorry matches her verdict, so the groove runs on, and you give up ground you could have held.

beats.text: “Dad says we're fine, like always. I'm the only one who worries.”
beats.cue: tired, looking at something across the room

lines.text: “What would you like Dad to do differently, Mum? Name one thing.”
lines.outcome: She laughs, short and sour. “Ask him to ring me, for once. He won't.”
lines.why: You turned her feeling into a request. A request is a cut she can answer, and it gives her a real choice instead of a rescue.

lines.text: “I'm sure Dad worries too, Mum. Don't upset yourself.”
lines.outcome: “Don't upset myself,” she repeats. “That's what everyone says.”
lines.why: This is the Caring Boss again, a matched volley that calms her and changes nothing. She hears no new message, so the whine comes back at the next line.

beats.text: “Then tell me it's not my fault. Just say it. Is it my fault?”
beats.cue: voice going thin, waiting for the yes

lines.text: “Nobody has to be at fault, Mum. What do you need from this call before we hang up?”
lines.outcome: A long breath. “Just to hear your voice on Sunday, I think.” She has said the real thing.
lines.why: Saying nobody is at fault is a cut, and it refuses to put anyone in the dock. The question after it gets her Pilot to answer, so a row has nothing to start from.

lines.text: “No, Mum, of course it isn't. It's not your fault.”
lines.outcome: “Good,” she says, and the call ends on a soft note. Nothing about Sunday has been decided.
lines.why: A matched volley that closes the question. It is kind, but it leaves the plea without a plan, so the same call comes back next week.

lines.text: “Fine, Mum, it's always about you, isn't it? Every single call.”
lines.outcome: Her voice goes up. “Don't you talk to me like that. Your father talks to me like that.” The phone goes quiet with a click.
lines.why: This is a verdict wrapped in a question. It invites her Boss to answer, and a person who is crossed tends to move into the seat the other one invited, so a row starts and the scene ends here.

items.payoff: The call ends early with the whine still on the line. Mum keeps the score, and next Sunday she starts from the last thing you said.

items.title: Wednesday, 22:40, the kitchen in apartment 3B
items.setting: The rent envelope is on the fridge, under a magnet shaped like a tea cup. Sam is still wearing his fintech lanyard, and he has not sat down.

beats.text: “I'm such an idiot. I forgot the rent again. Sorry, sorry, don't say it.”

lines.text: “Okay. When can you pay it, and how much can you do by Friday?”
lines.outcome: Sam stops with the envelope in the air. “Friday. Thursday, if I skip the tea.”
lines.why: You asked for a day and an amount, which is a cut from your Pilot that he can answer. The whine has nowhere to sit.

lines.text: “It's fine, Sam, don't worry about it.”
lines.outcome: He grins, relieved. “You're the best, seriously.” The envelope goes back on the fridge, with no date on it.
lines.why: You answered his Kid from the Caring Boss, which is a matched volley. He feels better at once, but the rent still has no day on it, and that is the price of the comfort.

beats.text: “You always know what to do. I'm hopeless with money, I'm the one who needs bailing out.”
beats.cue: a tight laugh, looking at the fridge and not at you

lines.text: “You're not hopeless, you're short this month. Give me the number and the day.”
lines.outcome: He pulls out his phone and shows you a figure. “Nine thousand now, the rest on the fourth.”
lines.why: You gave him a fact to answer, not a rescue. A grown-up can answer a number, and he did, so the talk stays open.

lines.text: “Give me the envelope. I'll sort it out, and you can pay me back later.”
lines.outcome: His shoulders drop. “You're a lifesaver. I owe you.” He hands over the envelope and forgets the date.
lines.why: You took the job off him. He is now the Kid being looked after, and you are carrying the rent, so the scene ends here.

lines.text: “Okay, but you're doing better than you think.”
lines.outcome: He laughs. “You say that every month.” The number is still unsaid.
lines.why: A kind word from the Caring Boss answers the feeling and never asks for the number. The number goes unsaid, so the rent stays where it was.

beats.text: “Fine, fine. Don't tell Gran, she'll make a whole speech out of it.”
beats.cue: half a smile, one hand up, testing whether you will keep his secret

lines.text: “I won't tell her. You tell her yourself on Sunday, before the watchman does.”
lines.outcome: He groans. “Fine. Sunday. I'll take the speech.”
lines.why: You kept the secret out of it and handed the choice back to him. Telling her himself keeps him an adult in the talk, and the rent does not become a family joke.

lines.text: “Deal. Our secret, and you owe me a tea.”
lines.outcome: He clinks his cup against yours. “Tea on me Friday, promise.”
lines.why: A secret makes the whine a shared joke, so the rent slides to next month with both of you laughing. It is pleasant, and the date stays unset.

beats.text: “Thanks. Sorry. Really, sorry, I'll sort it, promise.”
beats.cue: already halfway out of the kitchen, envelope under his arm

lines.text: “Don't say sorry. Say the day, and I'll write it on the fridge.”
lines.outcome: He laughs, takes the marker from the drawer, and writes “Fri” on the calendar with a smiley.
lines.why: You turned the sorry into a day that can be checked. He answers with something he can do, so the talk closes on an agreed day and the plea does not return on Thursday.

lines.text: “No problem, Sam. Sorted.”
lines.outcome: “Sorted,” he says, and he leaves. The envelope stays on the fridge with no date on it.
lines.why: A matched volley that closes the talk kindly, but no day has been set. Next week's sorry will sound the same.

items.payoff: Sam leaves the envelope with you, with a sticky note on it that says “Owe you”. The next sorry comes a week earlier.

items.who: You, after the call, working out why it held
items.text: “Okay. Ring me on Sunday, and tell me the one thing you want to talk about. I'll listen.”
items.cue: quieter now, the TV switched off
options: Her Pilot answered your Pilot, so the talk stayed open
Her Boss handed you a rule, so the whine returns
Her Kid gave up, so the call is over
items.why: Your request asked for a plan, so she answered with one. You changed seat, and the plea was cut before it could run on. A person who is crossed tends to move into the seat the other one invited, and your question invited her Pilot. A cut works when it asks for something real, like a day or one thing, and this one did.

traps.1: If her Boss had answered, it would sound like “Fine, ring on Sunday, and don't start again.” That is a rule handed back to you, and the whine would return next week with the rule attached.
traps.2: If her Kid had given up, it would sound like “Never mind, I'm being silly, forget I said it.” The call would end on the sulk, and the week would stay where it was.

items.example:
A sports coach at the nets: “Okay. Tell me one thing you want to fix before Saturday.”
The question has an end point, so the player has a real answer to give.

debrief.nadia: A plea calls on one seat, and if you answer from that same seat, the loop can run on and on. Changing seat to your Pilot cuts it, but the cut has to ask for something real, like a day or one thing she wants from you. Ask it as if you want the answer, because the same words said like a verdict will start a row.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a crossed transaction: the reply comes from a different ego state than the one addressed, or does not go back to the one that spoke, so communication breaks off until the vectors realign. The person who was crossed tends to shift into the ego state the other one invited.

reflection.prompt: Think of a message this week that asked you to make a feeling go away. Which seat did you answer from, and what would one plain question from your Pilot have opened instead?
